claims.text: A higher degree of local chemical ordering increases the activation barriers governing dislocation motion in multi-component concentrated alloys.
The increased barriers to dislocation motion caused by local chemical ordering raise yield strength relative to a near-random alloy.
Local chemical ordering enhances work hardening relative to a near-random atomic distribution.
A moderate-temperature aging treatment can promote local chemical ordering in the proposed alloy.
A high-temperature anneal can maintain or produce a near-random chemical configuration with minimal local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering produces spatial variations in stacking-fault and shear energies along dislocation glide paths.
The energy variations associated with locally ordered regions act as pinning or detrapping barriers for dislocations.
Locally ordered regions enhance cohesive interactions.
Locally ordered regions generate severe lattice distortions.
Local chemical ordering influences the selection of dislocation pathways involving slip, faulting, and twinning.
The LCO-treated alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the near-random baseline.
The LCO-treated alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in work-hardening rate relative to the near-random baseline.
The proposed effect should hold during ambient-temperature tensile deformation.
The proposed effect should hold in multi-component alloys where atomic-size differences and cohesive-energy variations are significant.
Matching grain size and extrinsic defect density between the heat-treatment groups isolates the degree of local chemical ordering as the controlled variable.
